docs.title: Atrium Platform
docs.text:
This site introduces the Atrium platform and covers your platform account: signing in, multi-factor authentication, and managing your password. One account signs you into every application in your environment.

  • About the Platform

    What Atrium is for, the problems it addresses, and its key design considerations.

  • Your Account

    Sign-in, authenticator setup, changing and recovering your password.

For using the environment itself, see your environment's own user guide — your operator will share its address.

For anything these pages don't answer, use your organisation's support route (linked from the sign-in page where configured).

docs.title: About the Atrium Platform
docs.text: Atrium is a platform your organisation runs to host secure research and teaching environments in the cloud. If you use one of those environments, you reach it through a single web address, sign in once, and work entirely in your browser — this page explains what sits behind that and why it is built the way it is.

docs.title: The problems it addresses
docs.text:
Sensitive data needs a safe place to be worked on. Research on health, social, or otherwise confidential data comes with obligations: the data must stay inside a controlled environment, everything that enters or leaves must be governed, and there must be a record of what happened. Atrium environments are built for exactly this — analysis happens inside the environment, not on personal machines, and data moves only through reviewed routes.

Secure environments are hard to build well, and harder to build repeatedly. Every new project needs the same foundations — private networking, identity, a hardened entry point, secrets handling, logging. Rebuilding those per project is slow and each rebuild is a fresh chance to misconfigure something. Atrium builds the shared foundations once, to one reviewed standard, and each environment plugs into them.

Cloud costs need governing as much as data does. Environments track spending against project budgets, and can be paused when not in use so idle infrastructure isn't billing.

docs.title: How it is put together
docs.text:
Three layers, each with a clear job:

  • A durable foundation of shared services — networking, secrets, logging, and the platform's stable public address.
  • A platform hub providing the single entry point, sign-in, and administration.
  • Modules — the environments people actually use. Each is self-contained and attaches to the platform rather than building its own foundations.

As a user you never see the layers: one address, one account, one browser.

docs.title: Key design considerations
docs.text:
• One front door. Everything is reached over HTTPS through a single hardened gateway; nothing else in the platform is exposed to the internet.
  • One identity. A single sign-on covers every application in your environment, with two-factor authentication required in secure environments. See Your Account.
  • Private by default. The platform's internal services — storage, secrets, infrastructure — are not reachable from the internet at all, only from inside the platform's own private network.
  • Governed data movement. In secure environments, data enters and leaves only through the governed, reviewed routes the environment defines, with every transfer recorded.
  • Everything as code. The whole platform is defined in reviewed, version-controlled code and stood up by automation — so environments are reproducible, and changes go through approval rather than ad-hoc edits.
  • Auditable. Platform actions and data movements are recorded centrally, so operators and governance teams can see what exists and what happened.
  • Cost-aware. Environments track project budgets and can be parked when idle.

docs.title: Using an environment
docs.text: Each environment publishes its own user guide covering its applications and day-to-day use — your operator will share its address alongside your sign-in details. For account matters (passwords, two-factor setup), see Your Account.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text: Open any application in your environment and you'll be taken to the platform sign-in page. Sign in once and you're signed in everywhere — all of your environment's applications share the same session.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
Your account arrives with a temporary password, given to you through a separate channel. On first sign-in you must choose your own password (minimum 12 characters with upper case, lower case, and a digit).

In secure (SDE) environments you'll also be asked to set up two-factor authentication: scan the QR code with an authenticator app (FreeOTP, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, or similar) and enter the code it shows. From then on, sign-in asks for your password plus the current code from your app.

docs.title: Changing a password you know
docs.text: Use the Account Console — from a signed-in session, open the account page (your operator can give you the direct address for your environment) and go to Account security → Signing in → Update password. This works entirely inside the platform; no email involved.

docs.title: Forgotten password
docs.text:
Depending on how your environment is configured, one of two routes applies:

  • Self-service reset — if the sign-in page shows Forgot password?, use it: a reset link is emailed to your registered address.
  • Operator-mediated reset — in stricter environments there is no self-service link; instead the sign-in page points at your organisation's support route. Raise a ticket, your identity is verified, and an operator sets a temporary password for you (you'll choose a new one at next sign-in).

docs.title: Lost authenticator
docs.text: If you lose access to your two-factor app, use your organisation's support route — an operator verifies your identity and resets your authenticator enrolment so you can set it up again at next sign-in.
